newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's central bank previews 1997 targets.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's central bank previews 1997 targets.

text.p: Heads of Colombia's central bank gave a sneak preview Thursday of the macroeconomic targets they are set to unveil Friday -- saying that 1997 would be a year of fiscal adjustment with more relaxed monetary and exchange rate policies.

At the National Agrarian Congress in Bogota, the bank's co-director Roberto Junguito said the target for the peso's devaluation against the dollar would be set at between 13 and 15 percent in nominal terms. This goal, he said was based on an inflation target of between 16 and 18 percent.

This year the peso has sunk less than three percent in nominal terms against the dollar, sparking a chorus of complaints from key export sectors whose ability to compete in the international market place has been undermined. The 1996 target was a 13.5 percent fall in the peso rate.
Inflation for 1996 is currently running at 21.87 percent, outsripping the year-end goal of 17 percent.
President Ernesto Samper, speaking at the same event, said public spending would increase 21 percent in nominal terms in 1997 -- about 10 percent lower than in each of the five previous years.
"The central bank's board of directors will agree to fiscal adjustment and a less strict monetary and exchange rate policy for 1997," Junguito said.

Junguito predicted foreign reserves will grow an added $1 billion in 1997 -- much of this is expected to come on the back of the highest-ever levels of oil exports. Reserves are currently around $8.3 billion.
He warned, however, that the government must exercise tight control over the levels of net foreign debt and said these should not exceed $1.7 billion if inflation was to be reined in.
The government had intended to ask the central bank for approval to place $1.8 billion in bonds abroad and seek an additional $1 billion in multilateral loans.
